children.text: Historical Simulation is the most intuitive of the three core VaR methods, and often the first one a desk builds. The idea is blunt: stop guessing what distribution returns follow, and just replay history against your current position. No normal distribution, no Student-t, no assumed shape at all. The data is the model.

body.label: Historical Simulation VaR
body.value: Apply each of the last N days' actual returns to today's position, revalue, sort the outcomes, and read off the percentile
body.context: It makes no assumption about the shape of the return distribution, whatever fat tails or skew existed in the data carry straight through.

children.text: Step by Step: Building Historical Simulation VaR

Four steps, always in this order. One, collect a series of historical returns for the position, typically 250 to 500 trading days of NSE close-to-close data. Two, apply each historical return to today's position size to generate a hypothetical profit or loss for that scenario. Three, sort all the hypothetical outcomes from worst to best. Four, pick the outcome at the percentile matching your confidence level, that is your VaR.

Here is a worked example with a deliberately small sample, 20 trading days, so every row is visible. A trader holds a Rs 10,00,000 Nifty futures position. These are the last 20 daily returns and the resulting hypothetical profit or loss on that position size.

body.caption: 20 daily returns applied to a Rs 10,00,000 position (illustrative)

children.text: Sort those 20 outcomes from worst to best: -32,000, -28,000, -15,000, -10,000, -7,000, -6,000, -5,000, -4,000, -3,000, -2,000, then the gains. With n = 20 days, the worst 5% of outcomes is exactly 1 observation, using the standard nearest-rank convention: index equals the ceiling of (1 minus confidence) times n.

body.caption: The nearest-rank convention: for 95% confidence and n = 20, rank equals ceiling of 0.05 x 20 = 1, so VaR is the single worst observation.

stats.label: 1-day 95% Historical VaR
stats.context: Rank 1 of 20, the single worst day

stats.label: 1-day 99% Historical VaR
stats.context: Also rank 1 of 20, identical to the 95% figure

body.text: Look closely at the 95% and 99% figures above, they are identical. With only 20 observations, ceiling(0.05 x 20) and ceiling(0.01 x 20) both equal 1, so there is no way to distinguish a 95% VaR from a 99% VaR, both just point at the single worst day in the sample. This is not a quirk of this example, it is a structural limitation of Historical Simulation with small samples. A believable 99% VaR needs enough observations that the 1% tail contains more than a handful of data points, which is exactly why real desks use 250 to 500 days, not 20.

children.text: Historical Simulation is only as good as the window it is built on, and that window can produce wildly different VaR figures for the exact same position depending purely on which trading days happen to fall inside it. Nothing illustrates this better than a Nifty VaR window that straddles March 2020.

body.caption: How the same 1-year Historical VaR window shifts around the COVID crash (illustrative, directionally accurate)

cells: A calm pre-COVID year, no extreme days
Low, around 1.3 to 1.6% of position value
Includes the full March 2020 crash and the circuit-breaker days
Sharply higher, easily 3 to 5x the December 2019 figure
March 2020 has mostly rolled out of the trailing 12 months

body.text: None of these three portfolios changed. The position on the desk was identical in all three cases. Only the calendar moved. This is the single biggest practical weakness of Historical Simulation: your risk number can swing hard purely because a specific stretch of trading days entered or exited a rolling window, with no change in the actual portfolio.

markDefs.definition: A Historical Simulation variant, sometimes called the BRW or hybrid approach after Boudoukh, Richardson and Whitelaw (1998), where more recent observations are given more influence in the ranking than older ones, using an exponential decay weight instead of counting every day equally.

children.text: The version worked through above treats every day in the window as equally important, a return from 495 days ago carries the same weight as yesterday's.

fixes this without throwing away the empirical, no-distribution-assumed approach: it assigns each historical day a weight that decays exponentially the further back it sits, so a recent sharp move contributes more to the ranking than an equally sized move from over a year ago.

body.caption: Weight assigned to the i-th most recent observation (i = 1 is yesterday), decay factor lambda, sample size n. Weights sum to 1 across the window.

columns.label: Equal-Weighted
points: Every day in the window counts identically
Simple to explain and to audit
A tail event dominates the VaR estimate for the entire window it sits in, then vanishes the day it rolls out
The version most textbooks introduce first

columns.label: Age-Weighted (BRW / Hybrid)
points: Recent days count more, older days fade gradually rather than dropping off a cliff
Smoother VaR behavior as the window rolls forward
Still keeps old tail events in the sample, just with less influence, unlike discarding them outright
One extra parameter, lambda, to choose and justify

body.title: Rank-Based VaR from a Larger Sample
body.prompt: A desk builds Historical Simulation VaR from n = 100 trading days on a Rs 20,00,000 position. Using the nearest-rank convention, what rank (i.e. the k-th worst observation) corresponds to the 95% 1-day VaR?
body.explanation: Rank equals ceiling of (1 - 0.95) x 100 = ceiling of 5 = 5. With 100 observations, the 95% VaR is the 5th worst day, a far more stable estimate than the single-observation cutoff you get with n = 20.

body.title: Explaining a VaR Spike to a Risk Committee
body.scenario: Your desk's 1-year equal-weighted Historical VaR on a Bank Nifty options book jumped from Rs 4 lakh to Rs 14 lakh overnight. The position itself did not change size or composition between yesterday and today.
body.prompt: What is the most likely explanation, and what would you check first?
body.modelAnswer: The most likely cause is that a single extreme historical day, probably a large down move, just entered the rolling lookback window, or possibly the exact rank used for the VaR calculation shifted onto a newly-included extreme day. Check the oldest and newest days that changed in the window between yesterday and today, and look specifically at whether a known stressed period, a circuit-breaker day, a large results-season gap, or similar, just rolled in or out. This is the defining fragility of equal-weighted Historical Simulation and is exactly why some desks prefer the age-weighted version, or cross-check against a parametric or Monte Carlo VaR that does not depend on a hard window edge.

body.text: Historical Simulation trades a distributional assumption for a window assumption. You stop guessing the shape of returns, but you start depending entirely on which specific days happen to be inside your lookback window.

points: Historical Simulation applies each of the last N days' actual returns to today's position, sorts the outcomes, and reads off the percentile, no assumed distribution required.
The nearest-rank convention, rank equals ceiling of (1 minus confidence) times n, means small samples cannot reliably separate a 95% VaR from a 99% VaR.
The same position can produce very different VaR figures purely because a stretch of extreme days, like March 2020, has entered or exited the rolling window, with no change to the actual portfolio.

Age-weighted, or BRW, Historical Simulation keeps the no-distribution-assumed approach but smooths this window fragility by decaying the influence of older observations instead of dropping them abruptly.
